notes.pump: Absorption peaks near 490 nm, so green lasers (532 nm) or direct blue/green diodes work. The ~3 µs upper-state lifetime makes flashlamps impractical.
notes.level: Vibronic 4-level: fast phonon relaxation empties the lower level, giving a very broad gain band.
notes.pumpWavelength: The absorption band spans ~400–600 nm; 532 nm from frequency-doubled Nd or Yb lasers is the classic pump.
notes.lasing: Gain spans ~650–1100 nm, among the broadest of any solid-state gain medium.
notes.transition: Ti³⁺ has a single 3d electron. ²E is the upper state; the lower ²T₂ is vibrationally broadened.
notes.modes: The huge bandwidth supports sub-10 fs pulses through Kerr-lens mode locking.
notes.power: Oscillators are pump-limited; chirped-pulse amplifiers reach mJ–J pulses (TW–PW peak power).
notes.apps: Ultrashort pulses plus tunability drive spectroscopy, microscopy, combs and high-field physics.
notes.lifetime: ~3.2 µs upper-state lifetime — short enough that a flashlamp pulse can't build inversion faster than the state decays, which is exactly why Ti:Sapph needs a CW or pulsed-laser pump instead.

modes.t: Sub-10 fs pulses from the oscillator

power.ok: W to kW average; Q-switched pulses of mJ–J

notes.pump: Flashlamps were the classic pump; diodes near 808 nm are now the workhorse.
notes.level: 4-level at 1064 nm: the lower ⁴I₁₁/₂ level empties fast. The 946 nm line is quasi-3-level.
notes.pumpWavelength: Nd:YAG absorbs strongly near 808 nm; 885 nm gives a lower quantum defect.
notes.lasing: 1064 nm is the strongest line, with weaker lines at 946 and 1319 nm.
notes.transition: The upper ⁴F₃/₂ level lives ~230 µs, ideal for energy storage.
notes.modes: Long upper-state lifetime makes Q-switching easy; the narrow gain (~0.6 nm) limits mode locking to ~ps.
notes.power: Scales from watts to kW; Q-switching gives ~10 ns pulses of mJ–J.
notes.apps: Robust and versatile: industry, medicine, ranging, and pumping via frequency doubling.
notes.lifetime: ~230 µs upper-state (⁴F₃/₂) lifetime. Long enough to store pump energy between flashlamp/diode pulses, which is what makes Q-switching to ns, mJ–J pulses straightforward.

modes.t: Sub-10 fs pulses from the oscillator

power.ok: Tens of W to multi-kW (thin-disk, rod)
no: Only nJ pulses at low power

notes.pump: Its narrow absorption line near 940 nm wastes most lamp light, so diode pumping is used in practice.
notes.level: Only two manifolds. The lower level sits in ²F₇/₂ and is thermally populated at room temperature, so it is quasi-3-level.
notes.pumpWavelength: 940 nm is broad and easy; the 969 nm zero-phonon line lowers the heat load.
notes.lasing: 1030 nm has a tiny quantum defect (~9%), so heating is low.
notes.transition: Yb³⁺ has just two manifolds: ²F₅/₂ → ²F₇/₂.
notes.modes: The ~9 nm bandwidth supports a few hundred fs, not sub-10 fs.
notes.power: Low heat load enables thin-disk lasers with multi-kW output.
notes.apps: High average power plus fs–ps capability make it the industrial ultrafast workhorse.
notes.lifetime: ~950 µs–1 ms upper-state lifetime — roughly 4× longer than Nd:YAG's. That extra storage capacity is a big part of why Yb:YAG scales so well in high-energy Q-switched and amplified systems.

notes.pump: A DC discharge excites He, which transfers energy to Ne by resonant collisions.
notes.level: The lower neon level (2p₄) empties quickly: a 4-level scheme.
notes.lasing: 632.8 nm dominates; other lines need different mirrors.
notes.transition: Both lasing states are excited neon levels (Paschen notation 3s₂ and 2p₄).
notes.modes: Low gain and little stored energy: HeNe lasers run CW with a very narrow linewidth.
notes.power: Low gain limits output to a few mW, but beam quality and coherence are excellent.
notes.apps: Superb coherence and beam quality suit alignment, metrology and interferometry.

modes.t: Sub-10 fs pulses from the oscillator

power.ok: ~10 W to tens of kW (cutting: 1–6 kW)

notes.pump: Discharge electrons excite N₂, which transfers energy to CO₂ by resonant collisions.
notes.level: The lower (10°0) vibrational level relaxes quickly, so it behaves as a 4-level laser.
notes.lasing: The vibrational-rotational bands sit at ~10.6 and ~9.4 µm.
notes.transition: From the asymmetric-stretch (00°1) to the symmetric-stretch (10°0) mode.
notes.modes: Narrow gain lines rule out fs pulses, but CW and TEA or Q-switched pulses are common.
notes.power: Efficiency of ~10–20% allows very high powers, up to tens of kW.
notes.apps: Mid-IR light is absorbed by many non-metals and tissue; pulsed CO₂ drives the Sn plasma for EUV.

modes.t: Sub-10 fs pulses from the oscillator

power.ok: Pulses of ~0.1 J to several J at a few Hz

notes.pump: Flashlamps are the classic pump; red laser diodes now allow diode pumping too.
notes.level: At room temperature it is a vibronic 4-level laser, like Ti:Sapph. The 680 nm R-line behaves as 3-level.
notes.pumpWavelength: Broad absorption in the yellow-green and red covers lamp output and red diodes.
notes.lasing: Tunable ~700–820 nm; 755 nm is the medical standard.
notes.transition: The vibronic ⁴T₂ band lases down to the ⁴A₂ ground state.
notes.modes: The upper-state lifetime (~260 µs) suits long pulses and Q-switching.
notes.power: Medical systems deliver about 0.1 J to several J per pulse at a few Hz.
notes.apps: 755 nm light is absorbed by melanin, hence hair and pigment treatments.
notes.lifetime: ~260 µs upper-state lifetime, similar in scale to Nd:YAG. Long enough to support both long free-running pulses and Q-switching.

pumpWavelength.ok: Blue-green, two bands near ~405 nm and ~530–550 nm

lasing.ok: 694.3 nm (R1 line; a weaker R2 line sits at 692.9 nm)

power.ok: Pulses of ~1 J to several J at low repetition rates (~1 shot/min to a few Hz)
no: Only nJ pulses at GHz rates

ok: Hair and pigment removal (older dermatology systems)

notes.pump: Two broad absorption bands (~405 nm and ~530–550 nm) overlap well with a xenon flashlamp's output; ruby is essentially always flashlamp-pumped.
notes.level: Ruby is the textbook pure 3-level laser: the lower laser level IS the ground state, so more than half the Cr³⁺ ions must be excited before any gain exists at all — unlike every quasi-3-level or 4-level laser elsewhere in this quiz.
notes.pumpWavelength: The two absorption bands sit in the blue and green-yellow, which is why ruby looks pink/red (it absorbs the complementary colors).
notes.lasing: 694.3 nm (R1) has higher gain and dominates; the weaker R2 line at 692.9 nm is rarely used.
notes.transition: Both the upper (²E) and lower (⁴A₂, ground state) levels are Cr³⁺ states in the sapphire crystal field — the same ion pair that gives alexandrite its R-line, but here it's the *only* lasing transition, not a side effect.
notes.modes: The long (~ms) upper-state lifetime lets ruby store energy for a flashlamp pulse, and early Q-switched ruby lasers were historically important, but the huge pump threshold of a 3-level system rules out practical CW operation.
notes.power: Modern ruby systems are mostly small (~1 J at low rep rate); historic large-aperture ruby amplifier chains reached much higher energies.
notes.apps: Ruby lasers have been largely displaced by better media, but its narrow, highly coherent pulsed red output is still used for holography and pulsed diagnostics.
notes.lifetime: ~3 ms metastable ²E lifetime — long for a solid-state laser, and part of why a single flashlamp pulse can invert enough population, but the true 3-level structure still demands very high pump energy.

pumpWavelength.ok: ~750–800 nm (Xe flashlamp bands; ~790 nm for diode/Ti:sapphire pumping)

modes.t: Direct sub-10 fs pulses from the oscillator

power.ok: Pulses of ~mJ to a few hundred mJ (research systems reach J-level)
no: Only nJ pulses at GHz rates

ok: Dental and dermatological procedures (skin resurfacing, ablation)

notes.pump: A xenon flashlamp's output overlaps Er:YAG's absorption bands around 500, 650 and 750–800 nm; diode or Ti:sapphire pumping near 790 nm is also used.
notes.level: Structurally the upper (⁴I₁₁/₂) and lower (⁴I₁₃/₂) laser levels are distinct from the ⁴I₁₅/₂ ground state, so it's labeled 4-level here — but see the lifetime note: this transition is unusually self-terminating, which the simple 3/4-level picture doesn't capture.
notes.pumpWavelength: The absorption bands are broad enough to tolerate either flashlamp or diode/Ti:sapphire pumping without precise wavelength matching.
notes.lasing: 2940 nm falls right in a strong water-absorption peak, which is exactly why it's so effective for tissue ablation.
notes.transition: Both levels belong to the ⁴I manifold family of Er³⁺, one level closer to the ground state than the ⁴I9/2 or ⁴S3/2 levels the flashlamp directly excites.
notes.modes: Continuous-wave operation is possible but requires high Er³⁺ doping so that ion-ion cross-relaxation keeps recycling the lower level fast enough.
notes.power: Energy per pulse is modest compared to Nd:YAG because of the self-terminating bottleneck; scaling further usually means higher doping and cross-relaxation, not just more pump power.
notes.apps: 2940 nm is the strongest water absorption band of any common laser line, which drives essentially all of its medical uses.
notes.lifetime: In heavily-doped crystals the upper level (⁴I₁₁/₂) lifetime is ~0.23 ms — but the lower level (⁴I₁₃/₂) lives even longer, so the 2.94 µm transition is inherently self-terminating. High Er³⁺ doping and cross-relaxation/up-conversion between neighboring ions are what rescue continuous or high-rep-rate operation — a genuinely different failure mode than the simple 3-level/4-level framework used elsewhere in this quiz.

modes.t: Direct sub-10 fs pulses from the oscillator

power.ok: Tens of W CW (rod/fiber); Q-switched pulses of mJ-level energy
no: Only nJ pulses at GHz rates

notes.pump: The ~785 nm absorption band (³H₆→³H₄) is reachable with the same AlGaAs diode technology used to pump Nd- and Ti:sapph-class lasers, or with a Ti:Sapphire laser in research setups.
notes.level: The terminal level (³F₄) sits close enough to the ground manifold (³H₆) to be thermally populated at room temperature, making this a quasi-3-level transition, the same category as Yb:YAG.
notes.pumpWavelength: 785–786 nm is host-dependent but close enough across Tm-doped crystals that the same diode designs are widely reused.
notes.lasing: The ~2 µm band is strongly absorbed by water and is considered eye-safe at typical operating energies, unlike 1064 nm or 1550 nm.
notes.transition: Both levels are excited-state manifolds of Tm³⁺; ³H₆ is also the ground manifold, which is why the lower level is thermally populated.
notes.modes: The very long upper-state lifetime supports efficient Q-switched energy storage even at modest diode pump power.
notes.power: Efficient cross-relaxation keeps thermal loading low relative to the stored energy, which is part of why Tm systems scale well in fiber and thin-rod geometries.
notes.apps: Eye-safety at 2 µm makes it attractive for LIDAR and outdoor ranging; strong water absorption suits soft-tissue surgery similarly to Er:YAG, just at a different wavelength and with fiber delivery more common.
notes.lifetime: ~15 ms radiative lifetime of the upper level in YAG — about 15× longer than Yb:YAG's. Combined with the two-for-one cross-relaxation process (one absorbed 785 nm pump photon excites two Tm³⁺ ions to the upper laser level), this gives a very low pump-power threshold for a given stored energy, and only a ~20% quantum defect despite the large wavelength gap between pump and laser photons.

lasers.name: Diode
lasers.gain: a direct-bandgap III-V semiconductor (e.g. GaAs/AlGaAs, as used in 808 nm pump-diode modules)

lasing.ok: ~808 nm (a common high-power pump-diode line; diode lasers overall span roughly 630–1600+ nm depending on composition)

lasers.transition: Direct band-to-band recombination across the semiconductor bandgap

modes.t: Directly modulated at GHz rates via the drive current
Q-switched via long-term energy storage in the gain medium

power.ok: mW (pointers, telecom) to tens of W per emitter; kW-class from diode bars/stacks
no: Only J-level pulses at low repetition rate

ok: Pump sources for other solid-state lasers (e.g. 808/940 nm modules)

notes.pump: Electrons and holes are injected directly across a forward-biased p–n (or heterostructure) junction — there is no separate optical or discharge pump step at all.
notes.level: Semiconductor gain doesn't come from discrete atomic energy levels: population inversion forms between the conduction and valence bands (or their quasi-Fermi levels) across the direct bandgap, so the atomic-style 3-level/4-level picture used for every other laser in this quiz simply doesn't apply.
notes.pumpWavelength: Not applicable: the excitation is electrical current, not light of any particular wavelength.
notes.lasing: The emission wavelength is set by the semiconductor's bandgap and alloy composition, not by a fixed atomic transition — 808 nm (GaAs/AlGaAs) is singled out here because it's the pump wavelength used throughout the rest of this quiz.
notes.transition: Gain comes from stimulated recombination of electrons and holes across the bandgap, not a transition between two discrete atomic energy levels like every other laser in this set.
notes.modes: The ns-scale carrier lifetime is too short to store meaningful energy for Q-switching, but it's exactly what allows the output to be turned on and off (modulated) at gigahertz rates by modulating the drive current.
notes.power: A single small emitter tops out around tens of W; today's highest-power diode systems stack many emitters into bars and arrays to reach kW-class output for pumping and industrial use.
notes.apps: Nearly every other laser in this quiz that's diode-pumped is ultimately powered by exactly this kind of device.
notes.lifetime: Carrier (spontaneous-emission) lifetime is typically ~1–3 ns — by far the shortest of any laser in this quiz. It rules out Q-switching or the µs–ms energy storage used by ion-doped crystals, but it's exactly why diode lasers can be modulated directly at GHz rates by modulating the drive current — the basis of fiber-optic data transmission.
